Today: why sequences need special models, how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) carry memory through time, why plain RNNs struggle to learn long-range dependencies (vanishing and exploding gradients), how LSTM and GRU gates help, and finally how the Transformer drops recurrence entirely and uses attention instead.

What is Sequence Data?

Data where the order matters. Prediction at any given time step is dependent on the previous steps.

Sequence Data Examples

  • Text (Language Translation, Predicting next word)
  • Time Series (Finance, Weather)
  • Music and Speech
  • DNA/Protein Sequences
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
A sequence is any data where order carries meaning. Shuffle the words of a sentence, the notes of a song, or the bases of a DNA strand and the meaning changes or disappears. The three animations: speech is a waveform over time, stock prices are a time series, and a language model writes one word at a time, each new word (in purple) depending on all the words before it. Ask the class: what other everyday data is sequential? (Video frames, sensor readings, clickstreams, handwriting strokes.)

Sequence Modeling Applications

To model sequences effectively, networks must:

  1. Handle variable-length sequences
  2. Track long-term dependencies
  3. Maintain order information or sequence order
  4. Share parameters across time / sequence

Challenges of modeling sequences:

  • Variable length inputs
  • Long-term dependencies
  • Order and context sensitivity
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
These four requirements are the design criteria we will check every model against. 1. Variable length: a tweet and a novel are both text. A fixed-size input layer cannot take both. 2. Long-term dependencies: in "The cat, which already ate a lot of food, was full", "was" agrees with "cat" many words earlier. 3. Order: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" contain the same words but mean different things. 4. Parameter sharing: what we learn about a word at position 3 should also apply at position 30.

Recurrent Neural Networks

Adding memory to a neural network

Section 2: from a feed-forward network that sees one input at a time, to a network that carries a memory from step to step.

Individual Timesteps

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Step through slowly. Start: one box, one input x_t, one output ŷ_t. Click 1: turn it on its side; time will run left to right. Click 2: apply the same network to every time step independently: ŷ_t = f(x_t). The problem: step 3 knows nothing about steps 0 to 2. For "predict the next word", that is useless. Click 3: pass a hidden state h from each step to the next. Now ŷ_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1}): the output depends on the current input and on a summary of the past. Click 4: the same thing drawn compactly as one cell with a loop. The loop is the recurrence; unrolling it gives the chain on the right.

Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)

The output of each time step depends on previous hidden states — memory through recurrence.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
This is a recurrent neural network. The hidden state h is the network's memory: at each step it is updated from the new input and the old hidden state, and it is passed forward. Click: the key phrase is "memory through recurrence". Ask: if h has, say, 128 numbers, can it remember a whole paragraph perfectly? (No. It has to compress, which is one of the limits we will meet later.)

Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)

The output of each time step depends on previous hidden states — memory through recurrence.

The same weights are reused at every step - parameter sharing across all the time steps

At each time step , for every input and hidden state

output vector
update hidden state
Keep state values stable since its squashes its input range [-1,1]
input vector
output vector
update hidden state
input vector
input to hidden weight matrix
hidden to hidden weight matrix
hidden to output weight matrix
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The two equations of a vanilla RNN. Update the hidden state: mix the new input (through W_xh) with the previous hidden state (through W_hh), then squash with tanh. Output: read the prediction off the hidden state through W_hy. Click 1: parameter sharing. W_xh, W_hh and W_hy are the same three matrices at every time step, so the number of weights does not grow with the sequence length. This is design criterion 4, and it is also what lets an RNN handle variable-length input (criterion 1). Click 2: the three weight matrices, labelled on the first cell. Click 3: why tanh? It squashes values into [-1, 1]. Without it, repeatedly multiplying by W_hh could make the hidden state grow without bound. Click 4: the same equations written with transposes, the convention used in many textbooks. Both forms say the same thing; only the shape convention of the matrices differs.

RNN for Sequence Modeling

Many to One

  • Sentiment Classification

One to Many

  • Text Generation
  • Image Captioning

Many to Many

  • Speech Translation

Key Design Criteria:

  1. Handle variable-length sequences
  2. Track long-term dependencies
  3. Maintain information about order
  4. Share parameters across the sequence
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The same RNN cell can be wired for different tasks, depending on where the inputs go in and where the outputs come out. Many to one: read a whole review, output one label (positive or negative). One to many: one input (an image, or a start token), many outputs (a caption, a generated text). Many to many: a sequence in, a sequence out (translation, forecasting the next values of a series). Click: the four design criteria again. An RNN meets 1, 3 and 4 by construction. Criterion 2, long-term dependencies, is where it struggles, as the next slides show.

Forward Propagation

Backward Propagation Through Time (BPTT)

Recall Backpropagation in Feed Forward Network
  1. Take the derivative (gradient) of the loss with respect to each parameter
  2. Adjust weights to shift parameters in order to minimize loss
Computing the gradient with respect to involves many factors of due to repeated gradient computation across time steps

When training an RNN, we use backpropagation through time — meaning we unroll the RNN over several time steps and propagate the error backwards through all those steps.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Forward pass: run the cell across the sequence, compute a loss L_t at every step, and add them up into the total loss L. Click 1: backward pass. The red arrows show the gradient flowing from L back through every step, including along the hidden-state chain from right to left. That is backpropagation through time: ordinary backprop on the unrolled network. The recall box lists the two steps of backprop from the last lecture. Click 2: to reach h_0, the gradient has to pass through every W_hh link in the chain. That means many multiplications by the same matrix, which is the source of the trouble on the next slide.

When computing gradients backward through time (BPTT), we repeatedly apply the chain rule

Where each term can be approximated as,

The gradient back to an early timestep involves multiplying many matrices together wherein each multiplication either amplifies or shrinks the gradient depending on the magnitude of these matrices

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The chain rule turns "how does the loss depend on an early hidden state" into a long product, one factor per time step. Each factor is roughly W_hh times the slope of the activation (tanh') at that step. So the gradient reaching h_0 is a product of T such factors, one per step: W_hh appears T times, each time scaled by the activation slope at that step. Intuition with plain numbers: 0.9 multiplied 50 times is about 0.005; 1.1 multiplied 50 times is about 117. A tiny difference per step becomes a huge difference over a long sequence.

If we look at the largest eigenvalue magnitude of

EigenvalueEffect on GradientsProblem
< 1Gradients shrink exponentiallyVanishing gradient
> 1Gradients blow up exponentiallyExploding gradient

.. challenge and limitation of RNN

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The size of the largest eigenvalue of that repeated factor decides what happens. Less than 1: every step shrinks the gradient, so early time steps get almost no learning signal. The network cannot learn long-term dependencies. This is the vanishing gradient. Greater than 1: every step multiplies it up, the gradient explodes, and training becomes unstable (loss jumps to NaN). A common fix is gradient clipping: cap the gradient's size before the update. Click: this is the core limitation of the plain RNN, and the motivation for gated models next.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
An interactive version of the eigenvalue table. The chart shows how much of the gradient from the loss at the last step survives back to each earlier step, on a log scale. The grey band is the "healthy" range. Ask the predict question first, then click to reveal: 0.9^50 ≈ 0.005 and 1.1^50 ≈ 117. Then drag the slider live: - 0.5: after 10 steps almost nothing is left; the network cannot learn anything that depends on words more than a few steps back. - 1.0: the knife edge, gradients neither vanish nor explode. Very hard to stay exactly here by tuning W_hh. - 1.2 and up: explosion, the loss becomes NaN. The fix there is gradient clipping. Gates (LSTM/GRU) and later attention are both ways of avoiding this long product.

Discussion

Recurrent Neural Networks

  1. Why can’t we just use a feed-forward network with a very large input layer to read a sentence?

    The input size would be fixed, so it cannot handle sentences of different lengths. It would also learn a separate weight for each position, so knowing what “cat” means at position 2 would not help at position 20. An RNN reuses the same weights at every step.

  2. In our hand example the memory fell from 0.762 to 0.090 in three steps. What would you change to make it last longer, and what is the risk?

    Increase toward 1. If it goes above 1, the hidden state saturates and, during training, gradients can explode. It is hard to make memory last long with a single repeated weight.

  3. Your RNN’s training loss suddenly becomes NaN. Which problem is this most likely to be, and what is a quick fix?

    Exploding gradients. Clip the gradient norm (for example clipnorm=1.0 in the Keras optimizer) or lower the learning rate.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Give pairs two minutes per question, take one or two answers, then click to reveal the suggested answer.

Gated RNNs: LSTM and GRU

Learning what to keep and what to forget

Section 4: gates as the fix for the vanishing gradient.

Gated Models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)

  • Are advanced RNN architectures designed to solve the limitations found in classic RNN using gates that regulate information that flow through the network
  • Mitigate vanishing and exploding gradient problems by controlling what to remember or forget
  • Still limited by sequential computation, since each timestep depends on the previous one

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

  • Memory system is implemented using gates:
    • forget (what information from previous cell state to discard)
    • input (what new information from the current input should be stored in the cell state),
    • output (what part of the current cell state is used to compute the next hidden state which is passed to the next time step)
  • Maintains a cell state (long-term memory) and a hidden state (short-term, working memory)
Analogy: the cell state is a student’s notebook. The forget gate erases old notes, the input gate writes new ones, and the output gate decides what to read aloud right now (the hidden state).

https://colah.github.io/posts/2015-08-Understanding-LSTMs/

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
An LSTM adds a second memory line, the cell state, that runs along the top of the diagram with only small, gated changes at each step. Because information (and gradient) can flow along it mostly unchanged, it does not vanish as quickly. Three gates, each a sigmoid that outputs a value between 0 and 1 (0 = block, 1 = let through): - forget gate: how much of the old cell state to keep - input gate: how much of the new candidate information to write - output gate: how much of the cell state to expose as the hidden state Note on terminology: the cell state is the long-term memory and the hidden state is the short-term (working) memory. (The original slide had these swapped.) In most references the cell state is described as the long-term memory and the hidden state as the short-term (working) memory.

Gated Models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)

  • Are advanced RNN architectures designed to solve the limitations found in classic RNN using gates that regulate information that flow through the network
  • Mitigate vanishing and exploding gradient problems by controlling what to remember or forget
  • Still limited by sequential computation, since each timestep depends on the previous one

Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)

  • Combine the input and forget gates of LSTM into a single update gate and reset gate
  • Maintains a single hidden state

https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The GRU is a simpler gated cell with no separate cell state. Update gate Z: how much of the old hidden state to keep versus replace with the new candidate. (It plays the role of the LSTM's forget and input gates together.) Reset gate R: how much of the old hidden state to use when computing the candidate. Fewer gates means fewer parameters and faster training; in practice LSTM and GRU often perform similarly. Both still process one time step after another, so they cannot be parallelized across the sequence. That is the opening for the Transformer.

Discussion

Gated RNNs

  1. In “The cat, which ate the fish my brother caught last week, was full”, which LSTM gate helps the model remember “cat” until it reaches “was”?

    The forget gate staying close to 1 keeps “cat” (singular) in the cell state across the long clause. The input gate wrote it in when “cat” was read, and the output gate exposes it when it is needed at “was”.

  2. GRU has fewer gates than LSTM. When might you pick GRU?

    When data or compute is limited: fewer parameters train faster and overfit less. In practice they often perform about the same, so try both.

  3. LSTM and GRU fix the vanishing gradient much better. What problem do they still not fix?

    They still read one step at a time, so training cannot be parallelised across the sequence and very long sequences are slow. That is the motivation for the Transformer.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Two minutes per question in pairs, then reveal. Question 3 is the bridge to the next section.

Attention and the Transformer

Every word looks at every other word, all at once

Section 5: attention, self-attention and the Transformer architecture.

Eliminating Recurrence: Attention is All You Need

In 2017, Vaswani et al. introduced a breakthrough paper titled “Attention Is All You Need”, proposing the Transformer architecture, which completely eliminated recurrence and relied solely on attention mechanisms to draw global dependencies between input and output.

By moving away from the sequential nature of RNNs, Transformers can process entire sequences in parallel using a novel concept known as self-attention.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The Transformer keeps the goal (model dependencies across a sequence) but drops the recurrence. Instead of passing a hidden state step by step, every word looks directly at every other word through attention. Two big wins: no long chain of multiplications between distant words (so long-range dependencies are easier), and all positions can be computed at the same time on a GPU (so training is much faster). This one diagram is the map for the rest of the lecture. We will walk through it piece by piece.

Running example

How an RNN and a Transformer Read the Same Sentence

RNN: one word per step

Transformer: all words in one step

Every word attends to every other word at the same time. “cat” (position 6) can look straight at “your” (position 1): one hop, not five.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The core difference in one picture. Top: the RNN has to wait for step 1 before step 2, and so on: six steps for six words. Information from "your" reaches the last "cat" only after passing through five hidden states, getting diluted each time (our hand example). Bottom: the Transformer computes all six positions together. Every pair of words is connected directly, so distance does not matter, and the work can be spread across a GPU. The trade-off to mention: attention compares every pair of words, so the cost grows with the square of the sentence length.

Input in English:
“The cat sat on the mat”

Output in Tagalog:
“Ang pusa ay umupo sa banig”

A transformer model uses attention to decide which English words are most relevant when generating each Tagalog word.

“The cat sat on the mat”

Word Being ProcessedOther Words It Attends ToWhy
satcatTo understand who sat
matTo understand where it sat
The, on, theLess important context

A transformer model uses self-attention to understand the relationship between words within the same sentence.

Model assigns attention weights -- higher values to more relevant words and lower values to less relevant ones.

Attention is a mechanism that models dependencies between different sequences when generating an output.

Self-Attention is a mechanism that models dependencies within the same sequence, allowing each position to relate to others and build contextual representations.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Two related ideas. Attention (between sequences): while writing "pusa", the translator should look mostly at "cat"; while writing "banig", mostly at "mat". Click: self-attention (within one sequence): to understand "sat", the model looks at "cat" (who sat) and "mat" (where), and gives little weight to "the" and "on". Ask the class: in "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", which word should "it" attend to? What if we change "tired" to "wide"?

The self-attention mechanism allows a model to understand the relationships between words in a sentence, regardless of their distance from each other. It works by computing a score that determines how much focus each word should have on every other word in the sentence.

Attention is a mechanism that models dependencies between different sequences when generating an output.

Self-Attention is a mechanism that models dependencies within the same sequence, allowing each position to relate to others and build contextual representations.

The key mathematical building blocks of self-attention are three learned vectors derived from each input token:

  1. Query (Q) - what the token is looking for in other tokens
  2. Key (K) - properties of other tokens to be compared with the query
  3. Value (V) - information that will be passed along based on how much attention the query places on each key
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The movie-lookup analogy. Think of a Python dictionary: keys are genres, values are movies. A normal dictionary needs an exact key match. Attention is a soft lookup: the query "love" is compared with every key, matches "romantic" strongly and the others weakly, and returns a weighted blend of all the values, mostly Titanic. Click: in self-attention, each word produces all three vectors from its own embedding, using three learned weight matrices: - Query: what am I looking for? - Key: what do I offer? - Value: what do I pass on if selected? The formula says: compare queries with keys (QKᵀ), scale, turn the scores into weights with softmax, and use the weights to average the values.

Eliminating Recurrence: Attention is All You Need

The Transformer model consists of two main parts: the encoder and the decoder which work together for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

The encoder processes the input sequence and captures its most important features, while the decoder uses this information to generate the output sequence.

Together, they enable the model to identify and attend to the most relevant parts of the input when producing an accurate output.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Left tower (pink): the encoder reads the whole input sentence at once and turns every word into a context-aware vector. Right tower (green): the decoder writes the output one word at a time, looking at what it has written so far and at the encoder's vectors. "Nx" means the block is stacked N times; the original paper used N = 6. Modern models often use only half: BERT is encoder-only (good for understanding text), GPT is decoder-only (good for generating text).

Transformer Architecture: Encoder

The encoder takes in a sequence and processes it in several layers. Each layer consists of two main components: multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward neural network.

Input Embedding

Each word in the input sequence is first mapped to a unique position in a predefined vocabulary — a collection of all words the model has learned during training.

Every word is assigned a unique ID or index, which is then converted into a dense numerical vector called an embedding.

These embeddings represent the semantic meaning of words in a high-dimensional space. In this space, each word corresponds to a unique vector representation, allowing the model to measure similarity and relationships between words based on distance and direction in vector space.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Computers need numbers, so each word becomes a vector. Step 1: look up the word's ID in the vocabulary ("CAT" is 6587 every time it appears, which is why both CATs get the same column). Step 2: use the ID to pick a row from a learned embedding table: a list of 512 numbers. Words with similar meanings end up close together. In the small picture, dog and cat are near each other, and car is far away. The model learns these positions during training. (The numbers in the table are illustrative.)

Transformer Architecture: Encoder

The encoder takes in a sequence and processes it in several layers. Each layer consists of two main components: multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward neural network.

Positional Encoding

Transformers process all words in a sequence simultaneously. To preserve the position and order of words, the model adds a positional encoding to each word embedding using sine and cosine functions.

Sine and cosine functions create smooth, repeating numerical patterns that encode word positions that give the Transformer a built-in sense of sequence order, even though it processes all words in parallel.

Each position (word order) gets a unique pattern of sine and cosine values that form unique “signatures” for every position

  • Lower dimensions use slower wave patterns (long wavelengths)
  • Higher dimensions use faster oscillations (short wavelengths)

Sine and cosine are continuous and periodic, the model can easily learn relative positions and reconstruct word and order relationships.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Problem: attention looks at all words at once, so on its own it has no idea which word came first. "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical. Fix: add a position signal to each embedding. Notice the two CATs: same embedding, but different positional encodings (position 1 and position 5), so the model can tell them apart. Click: the sine/cosine formula. Each dimension is a wave of a different speed. Low dimensions change slowly with position (like the hour hand of a clock), high dimensions change fast (like the second hand). Together, the readings of all the "hands" give each position a unique signature, and nearby positions get similar signatures.

Interactive

Positional Encoding: Waves of Different Speeds

Each dimension of the positional encoding is a sine or cosine wave. The first dimensions change fast; later dimensions change more and more slowly.

Drag the position

3

Its “signature” (dims 0–7)

Analogy: the hands of a clock. The second hand moves fast, the hour hand slowly. Reading all the hands together gives every moment a unique time, just as all the waves together give every position a unique signature.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Live version of the PE formula with d_model = 16 (the real model uses 512). Drag the position slider: the vertical line moves across the waves and the colored cells on the right show the values the model adds to that word's embedding. Points to make: - Neighbouring positions (3 and 4) have similar signatures; distant ones (3 and 30) look very different. That lets the model reason about "nearby" versus "far". - The fast waves (top: dims 0 and 1) distinguish neighbouring positions; the slow waves (bottom) distinguish far-apart positions. Each sine has a cosine partner at the same speed. - Values stay between −1 and 1, so they do not drown out the word embedding.

The self-attention mechanism allows a model to understand the relationships between words in a sentence, regardless of their distance from each other. It works by computing a score that determines how much focus each word should have on every other word in the sentence.

The key mathematical building blocks of self-attention are three learned vectors derived from each input token:

  1. Query (Q) - what the token is looking for in other tokens
  2. Key (K) - properties of other tokens to be compared with the query
  3. Value (V) - information that will be passed along based on how much attention the query places on each key
Analogy: a library search. The query is what you type in the search bar, the keys are the titles and tags on every book, and the values are what is inside the books. Attention borrows a little from every book, more from the best matches.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Back to self-attention, now that the input (embedding + position) is ready. Each word's input vector is multiplied by three learned matrices, W_Q, W_K and W_V, to get its query, key and value. Quick check for the class: why three different vectors instead of one? Because "what I am looking for" and "what I offer to others" are different things. A pronoun looks for a noun, but offers itself as a pronoun.

Transformer Architecture

Multi-head self-attention

The key mathematical building blocks of self-attention are three learned vectors derived from each input token:

  1. Query (Q) - what the token is looking for in other tokens
  2. Key (K) - properties of other tokens to be compared with the query
  3. Value (V) - information that will be passed along based on how much attention the query places on each key
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Where this lives in the architecture: the "Multi-Head Attention" block at the bottom of each encoder layer. The next three slides compute that formula step by step on the sentence "your cat is a lovely cat".

Each row in this matrix captures not only the meaning (given by the embedding) or the position in the sentence (represented by the positional encodings) but also each word’s interaction with other words.

To compute the attention score between two words, the dot product of the Query vector of one word and the Key vector of another is calculated. This score represents the relevance of the second word to the first.

These scores are then scaled (by dividing by the square root of the vector dimension) to prevent very large values. This also helps stabilize the gradients during training.
A softmax function is applied to turn these scores into probabilities. Each row now sums to 1 — showing how much attention each word gives to others.

Finally, we use these attention weights to combine the value vectors.
This produces the contextualized representation for each word — meaning each word’s vector now includes information from other relevant words in the sentence.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Six words, each with a 512-number query and key. Step 1: Q × Kᵀ gives a 6 × 6 table of scores: row = the word asking, column = the word being looked at. A big dot product means the query and key point the same way: relevant. Click 1: divide by √512 ≈ 22.6 so the scores don't get so large that softmax becomes all-or-nothing (which would make the gradients tiny). Then softmax each row so it sums to 1. Read a row aloud: "LOVELY" gives its biggest weight (0.227) to itself and the next to the second "CAT" (0.174). Click 2: multiply the 6 × 6 weights by V (6 × 512). Each word's new vector is a weighted average of all the value vectors. Same shape as the input, but now every word carries context.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The attention formula with numbers small enough for the board. To keep it short we take the query, keys and values as given (in a real model they come from multiplying the embeddings by W_Q, W_K and W_V). Click 1: dot products. q·k for "a" = 1·0 + 0·1 = 0; for "lovely" = 1·2 + 0·0 = 2; for "cat" = 1·1 + 0·0 = 1. Click 2: divide by √d_k = √2 ≈ 1.414. (It would get the same weight as "cat".) The notebook (part 4) checks these numbers in code.

Transformer Architecture

Multi-head Attention

An extension of self-attention

Allows the model to look at the input from different perspectives by splitting the attention mechanism into multiple parallel "heads."

Each head processes the sentence independently, focusing on different aspects or relationships.

Analogy: several reviewers read the same essay. One checks grammar, one checks the argument, one checks the references; their notes are combined at the end. Each head is one reviewer.

While self-attention provides valuable insights into word relationships, it might not capture every possible feature of a word, such as its role as a noun, verb, or even an adjective depending on the context. This is where multi-head attention comes in, as an extension of self-attention.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
One attention pattern per layer is limiting: a word relates to others in several ways at once (grammar, meaning, coreference, position). Multi-head attention runs several attention computations side by side, each with its own learned W_Q, W_K, W_V. One head might learn "which noun does this adjective describe", another "which word does this pronoun refer to". Analogy: a panel of reviewers reading the same essay, each checking something different, then combining their notes.

Transformer Architecture

Multi-head Attention

The input embeddings are first linearly projected into multiple smaller sets of Query, Key, and Value vectors, each corresponding to a different "head."

Each head independently applies the self-attention mechanism. So, if we have 8 heads, the model applies self-attention 8 times, each time on different projections of the Query, Key, and Value vectors

The outputs from all the heads are then concatenated and passed through a final linear layer, which merges them into a single output vector.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Follow the diagram left to right. 1. The input is multiplied by W_Q, W_K and W_V, and each result is split into h smaller pieces, one per head. With d_model = 512 and 8 heads, each head works with 64 numbers. Click 2. Each head runs the same attention formula on its own slice. The small visualization on the right shows one head: the word "making" attends strongly to "more difficult". Click 3. The 8 outputs (8 × 64 = 512 numbers per word) are joined back together and multiplied by W_O to mix the heads' findings. Cost is about the same as one big head, because each head is smaller.

Transformer Architecture

Feed-Forward Network

In each layer of the Transformer, a Feed-Forward Network (FFN) is applied to every word independently.

It consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between, which introduces non-linearity and helps the model capture complex patterns.

  • First Linear Transformation: The input word representation (often 512 dimensions in size) is first passed through a linear transformation, which projects it to a higher-dimensional space (typically 2048 dimensions).
  • ReLU Activation: After the first transformation, a ReLU activation is applied to introduce non-linearity. This non-linear step allows the model to learn more complex patterns and relationships in the data.
  • Second Linear Transformation: The ReLU output is then passed through a second linear transformation, which projects it back to the original dimensionality (usually 512).
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
After attention has mixed information between words, the FFN processes each word on its own: expand 512 → 2048, ReLU, shrink 2048 → 512. The same FFN weights are applied to every position. A way to say it: attention is where words talk to each other; the FFN is where each word thinks about what it heard. FFN(x) = max(0, x·W1 + b1)·W2 + b2, exactly the dense layers from the first lectures.

Transformer Architecture

Add & Norm

Combination of residual connection and layer normalization applied to a sublayer (Multi-Head Attention or Feed Forward)

Residual Connection (Add)

Instead of feeding only the output of the layer into the next layer, input is added to the output

This allows the network to preserve the original information and helps gradients flow more easily during backpropagation (mitigating the vanishing gradient problem)

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The residual (skip) connection: output = input + what the sublayer computed. The sublayer only has to learn a correction, not rebuild the whole representation. It also gives the gradient a shortcut: the derivative of x + Sublayer(x) with respect to x is 1 + (something), so even if the sublayer's gradient is small, the 1 lets the signal pass straight through. Compare with the RNN, where the gradient had to go through W_hh again and again.

Transformer Architecture

Add & Norm

Combination of residual connection and layer normalization applied to a sublayer (Multi-Head Attention or Feed Forward)

Normalization

After adding we apply layer normalization to stabilize and scale the vector

This standardizes the inputs to a layer so that they have zero mean and unit variance.

Input: [1, 10, 100, 1000]

The large differences makes it hard for the layer to learn because weights have to adjust to different scales.

Zero mean: the average becomes 0
[1, 2, 3] the mean is 2. Subtract it.
[-1, 0, 1] the values are centered around zero.

Unit variance: the spread is scaled so the variance is 1
[1, 0, 1] squared deviations.
(1+0+1)/3 = 0.667 the variance; std = √0.667 ≈ 0.816.
[-1, 0, 1] / 0.816 = [-1.22, 0, 1.22] now the variance is exactly 1.

Neural networks work best when inputs are on a similar scale.

Variance = 1 ensures that no feature is too big or too small, which keeps learning stable and efficient.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Layer normalization rescales each word's vector to mean 0 and variance 1 (then applies a learned scale and shift). Worked through with [1, 2, 3]: - mean = 2, so subtracting gives [-1, 0, 1] - squared deviations [1, 0, 1], variance = 2/3 ≈ 0.667 - divide by the standard deviation √0.667 ≈ 0.816 to get about [-1.22, 0, 1.22], whose variance is exactly 1. "Add & Norm" appears after every sublayer in both encoder and decoder.

Discussion

Attention

  1. Without positional encoding, would the Transformer see any difference between “your cat is a lovely cat” and “cat lovely a is cat your”?

    No. Self-attention only compares vectors, so shuffling the words just shuffles the rows. Positional encoding is what gives the model a sense of order.

  2. Why do we divide by before the softmax?

    With 512 dimensions, dot products get very large. Softmax of large numbers puts almost all the weight on one word and its gradient becomes almost zero, so learning stalls. Scaling keeps the scores in a reasonable range.

  3. A sentence twice as long has how many more attention scores to compute?

    Four times as many: every word is compared with every word, so the cost grows with . This is why long documents are expensive for Transformers.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Two minutes per question in pairs, then reveal.

Transformer Architecture: Decoder

The decoder in a transformer model consists of several layers, each with three main components that work together to generate output sequences based on the encoded input and previously generated tokens.

Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention

The first attention mechanism in the decoder. Similar to self-attention in the encoder but with masking.

Future positions in the sequence are masked to ensure that each position in the output can only attend to previous positions.

E.g

While generating "IS," the model would only be allowed to attend to "YOUR" and "CAT," but not to "A," "LOVELY," or the second "CAT."

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The decoder has three sublayers: masked self-attention, cross-attention, and a feed-forward network, each followed by Add & Norm. Click: masking. When the decoder predicts word 3, it must not peek at words 3, 4, 5 and so on, or training would be cheating: the answer would be in the input. In the attention score table, all the future cells are set to minus infinity before the softmax, so their weights become 0. The animation shows which earlier words each position may look at.

Transformer Architecture: Decoder

The decoder in a transformer model consists of several layers, each with three main components that work together to generate output sequences based on the encoded input and previously generated tokens.

Multi-Head Cross-Attention

“The next sub-layer performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack.”

Connects the encoders output to the decoder.

Allows the decoder to attend to the full context of the input sequence from the encoder while generating each word in the output sequence.

In this layer:

  • The Query (Q) comes from the decoder’s output (after masked self-attention).
  • The Key (K) and Value (V) come from the encoder’s output.

Cross-attention to distinguish from self-attention because it attends to a different sequence which is the encoder’s output rather than the decoder’s output.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Cross-attention is the bridge between the two towers, and it is the "attention between different sequences" from earlier. The decoder asks (queries): "I am about to write the next Tagalog word; which English words matter now?" The encoder's vectors answer as keys and values. While writing "pusa", the weights should land mostly on "cat". Point to the arrow in the diagram that carries the encoder output into the middle block of the decoder.

Transformer Architecture: Decoder

At the start of the training, the input to the decoder masked multi-head attention comes from target sequence shifted right.

Target sequence: your cat is a lovely cat </s>
Decoder input: <s> your cat is a lovely cat

Decoder InputDecoder
Predicts
(Target)
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
"Shifted right" means the decoder input is the target sentence with a start token <s> added at the front. So at every position, the input is "everything so far" and the label is "the next word". With masking, all seven rows of this table are trained at once in a single pass. This is called teacher forcing: during training the decoder sees the true previous words, not its own guesses. At inference time there is no target, so the model generates one word, appends it, and runs again.

Transformer Architecture: Decoder

Linear & Softmax

The decoder’s output is passed through a linear transformation and a softmax layer to produce a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary. The word with the highest probability is selected as the next word in the sequence

In the model, a true token is represented as a one-hot vector.

probability_vector = [0.1,0.2,0.5,0.1,0.1]
target_vector = [0,0,1,0,0]

Loss is small if correct token has high probability, large if low

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
The last step turns the decoder's 512-number vector into one score per vocabulary word (the Linear layer), then into probabilities (softmax). The loss is cross-entropy: because the target is one-hot, only the probability of the correct word matters, and the loss is −log of it. - p = 0.5 gives 0.693 (this example, natural log) - p = 0.9 would give 0.105 - p = 0.1 would give 2.303 So the model is pushed to put more probability on the right word. This is the same cross-entropy from the first lecture, just over a whole vocabulary.

Discussion

The Transformer

  1. Why does the decoder need masking during training but the encoder does not?

    The decoder learns to predict the next word, so it must not see the answer. The encoder only reads the input sentence, which is fully known, so every word may look at every other word.

  2. What would go wrong if we removed the residual (Add) connections from a 6-layer Transformer?

    Gradients would have to pass through every sublayer, so deep stacks would train poorly (the vanishing problem again), and each layer would have to rebuild the whole representation instead of adding a correction.

  3. ChatGPT is a decoder-only Transformer. Which blocks from today’s diagram does it keep, and which one does it drop?

    It keeps masked self-attention, the feed-forward network, Add & Norm, and the Linear + Softmax output. It drops the encoder, and so also the cross-attention, because there is no separate input sentence to attend to.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Sequence Modeling
Two minutes per question in pairs, then reveal. Question 3 links today's architecture to tools students already use.

Summary: RNN vs LSTM/GRU vs Transformer

RNNLSTM / GRUTransformer
1. Variable-length sequencesYes: one step per wordYesYes (up to a maximum length)
2. Long-term dependenciesWeak: gradients vanishBetter: gates protect the memoryStrong: any two words are one step apart
3. Order informationBuilt in (reads in order)Built inAdded via positional encoding
4. Parameter sharingSame weights every time stepSame weights every time stepSame weights every position
Parallel trainingNo: step by stepNo: step by stepYes: all positions at once
Cost for long inputsGrows with Grows with Grows with

The four design criteria from the start of the lecture are rows 1–4.
